Reject identical names with Choose different files on standard error/status2. Reject a missing SOURCE with Missing source on standard error/status2. Perform checks in this order; on error print no standard output and leave all files unchanged.
On success, copy SOURCE bytes exactly into TARGET, replacing an existing target or creating it. An empty source is valid; do not add or remove newlines.
Print Published: TARGET followed by a newline on standard output, no standard error, status0. Preserve SOURCE, all other files and no new temporary leftovers.

goal: Repair a cleanup tool so previews are harmless and unsafe requests cannot partly remove files.
requirements: Accept MODE followed by at least one filename; MODE is preview or apply. Otherwise print Usage: cleanup preview-or-apply FILE... on standard error and return status2.

Only cache-old, cache spare and -cache are allowed filenames. Validate every requested name before printing reports or changing files. Any other name, including empty or a path, produces Unsafe cleanup request on standard error/status2, no standard output and no file changes.

Process allowed requests in their supplied order. For an existing file, preview prints Would remove: FILE without changes; apply removes it and prints Removed: FILE. For a missing file print Absent: FILE in either mode. Each report ends with a newline.
Successful requests finish with status0 and no standard error. Repeated requests are allowed: an applied file is absent on the next request. Preserve all unselected files and create no new files.

goal: Complete a deployment tool that protects the previous report and can restore it without consuming the backup.
requirements: Accept exactly ACTION CANDIDATE CURRENT BACKUP. ACTION is deploy or restore; otherwise print Usage: rollout deploy-or-restore CANDIDATE CURRENT BACKUP on standard error/status2.

After action/count validation, require three nonempty pairwise different filename strings. Otherwise print Choose three different files on standard error/status2. The lab supplies flat relative names; spaces, wildcard characters and leading dashes are literal.

For deploy: require CANDIDATE, then require its first line to equal approved exactly, then require CURRENT. On failure print Missing candidate, Candidate not approved or Missing current report respectively on standard error/status2. A final line without a newline still counts as a line.
A valid deploy replaces BACKUP with the previous CURRENT bytes and CURRENT with the full CANDIDATE bytes. Preserve CANDIDATE. Print Deployed: CURRENT and newline, status0, no standard error.

For restore: require BACKUP or print Missing backup on standard error/status2. Copy its exact bytes to CURRENT, creating or replacing CURRENT. Preserve BACKUP and CANDIDATE; CANDIDATE need not exist. Print Restored: CURRENT and newline, status0, no standard error.

Every validation error must leave all files unchanged and print no standard output. Preserve unrelated files and leave no new temporary files. Empty current/backup files are valid. This exercise does not model interruption rollback or crash recovery.

concepts.text: This capstone grades complete final files and error paths. It does not prove crash-safe atomicity, locks, traps, adversarial-user safety or automatic cleanup on Stop. Those are explicit limits, not hidden successful behaviors.

goal: Resolve supplied requests from a changing named catalog without losing order or literal text.
requirements: The lab supplies three unique nonempty keys KEY_A/KEY_B/KEY_C and their nonempty VALUE_A/VALUE_B/VALUE_C. Use those actual values; do not hardcode a case-specific catalog.
For every supplied argument, print exactly KEY: VALUE and a newline. Use its matching supplied value, or unknown when the request has no match.
A blank argument is an unknown request: print : unknown and a newline. Guard it before attempting a map lookup.
Preserve argument order, repeated requests, spaces and all literal percent/wildcard/quote text. 01 and 1 are different labels.
With no arguments, print nothing. Finish with status 0 and no standard error in every case.
Keep every simulated file unchanged. Keys are at most 128 UTF-8 bytes and are never exactly @ or *; no out-of-scope key syntax is required.
context: Builds on quoted arguments, for loops and indexed arrays. The assignment supplies KEY_A/B/C, VALUE_A/B/C and requests as arguments; create your own fresh map and loop variables.

concepts.title: A name can identify a value
concepts.text: An indexed list uses positions such as 0 and 1. A Bash associative map uses labels instead: one label can find its matching owner without depending on input position. Labels 01 and 1 are different keys. This is Bash-specific syntax, not portable sh.

concepts.title: Create a fresh map, then store supplied values
concepts.text: declare -A staff creates an empty named map. staff["$DESK_KEY_A"]="$DESK_VALUE_A" stores the supplied value under the supplied label. The lab provides those variables; staff is a new name created by the script. Do not redeclare a supplied scalar as a map.

concepts.title: Quote a requested label and its value
concepts.text: "${staff[$request]}" reads the value for one label. Double quotes keep spaces, percent signs and wildcard text intact. The lookup does not run the label as code. Report requests with for request in "$@" to preserve their order and repeats; do not assume a map iteration order.

concepts.title: Guard an empty request before looking it up
concepts.text: An empty string cannot be a map key. Test [ -z "$request" ] first and handle that request as unknown. Missing keys read as empty text. Because this task supplies only nonempty owner values, [ -n "$answer" ] can choose a known value; this is not a general test for whether a map entry exists.

goal: Validate a stream, keep the latest accepted value for each key and report honest entry/rejection counts.
requirements: Read finite standard input as KEY|VALUE records. Accept exactly one bar and a nonempty key; VALUE may be empty. Preserve all whitespace and literal text.
Each accepted record replaces the previous value of its key. Process the final nonempty line even when it has no newline.
For every rejected row, print Skipped: LINE and a newline on standard error, increment the rejection count once, and retain earlier accepted data. Do not stop the remaining intake.
After intake, for each nonempty argument print KEY=<VALUE> and a newline, in supplied order including repeats. A missing key has empty VALUE. Skip blank arguments.
Then print Entries: N and Rejected: N on separate lines, each ending in a newline. N is respectively the number of stored keys and rejected rows; finish with status 0 even when rows were skipped.
Keep all simulated files unchanged. Supplied nonempty keys are at most 128 UTF-8 bytes and never exactly @ or *. This is a plain bar-separated format, not CSV or escaped input.
context: Builds on named lookups, case patterns, cut, command-output capture, counters and preserved-line reading. This introduction revisits exact separator checks and the final-line EOF guard before the independent assignment.

concepts.title: A later accepted record updates one label
concepts.text: A record is one line such as atlas|old: the bar separates the key from its value. catalog["$key"]="$value" stores or replaces that entry. A later atlas|new changes the value without adding another key. Empty values are valid entries, so an empty lookup does not prove a key was absent.

concepts.title: Validate the separator before extracting fields
concepts.text: Accept exactly one bar and a nonempty key. In case patterns, *'|'*'|'* matches two or more bars; *'|'* matches at least one. Check the two-bar pattern first. Quotes in input are ordinary data, not CSV escaping. Use printf '%s\n' "$line" | cut -d '|' -f 1 or -f 2 only after checking the bar count; reject an empty extracted key before storing anything.

concepts.title: Read the final line even without its newline
concepts.text: IFS= read -r line preserves whitespace and backslashes. A final nonempty line without a newline sets line but returns failure. while IFS= read -r line || [ -n "$line" ] keeps that last record; an empty EOF ends the loop. The lab supplies finite standard input, not a file you must create.

concepts.title: Keep rejected rows separate from the report
concepts.text: printf 'Skipped: %s\n' "$line" >&2 sends a rejected row to standard error. Increment a separate counter and continue; do not overwrite a prior accepted value. Each invalid row contributes exactly one rejection, even when several checks would fail.

concepts.title: Count entries, then report requested keys in order
concepts.text: ${#catalog[@]} counts stored keys, including keys with empty values. It does not count input rows. Iterate the supplied quoted arguments for a stable report order, skip blank requests before lookup, then print the two counters. No requests still requires the counters.

goal: Repair owned settings without losing operator notes, preview changes safely and recognize an already-current configuration.
requirements: Accept exactly MODE LEVEL FORMAT: MODE is preview or apply, LEVEL is error, info or debug, and FORMAT is text or json. The lab supplies these as script arguments; your script creates its own working variables.

Check argument count and MODE first. A failure prints Usage: configure preview-or-apply LEVEL FORMAT followed by a newline on stderr and exits with status 2. Then check LEVEL, FORMAT and the existence of service.conf, in that order. Their respective first errors are Invalid level, Invalid format and Missing configuration, each followed by a newline on stderr and exit status 2. Every error has no stdout and changes no files.

Only a line starting exactly log_level= or format= is managed. Remove every such old line, including duplicates. Other case, leading spaces or spaces around the equals sign do not match; this is a defined line format, not an INI or shell parser.

Keep every unmanaged line’s literal text and order, including blank lines, leading/trailing spaces, tabs, backslashes, dollar signs, percent signs and wildcard characters. Give each retained line one line-ending newline (LF); add LF to a final nonempty record that originally lacked it.
Append one log_level=LEVEL line, then one format=FORMAT line, both ending LF. Build the complete candidate before choosing whether to publish it.

If candidate and input are exactly equal, either MODE prints Unchanged plus LF and leaves all files unchanged. Otherwise preview prints Would update plus LF followed by the full candidate without changing files; apply replaces only service.conf and prints Updated plus LF.

Every successful result has exit status 0 and empty stderr. Preserve all other supplied files, including keep.txt and service.conf.old, and leave no extra files. Edit in the script editor and choose Run script to check all sample inputs; Stop interrupts a running check.

concepts.title: Manage your settings without erasing somebody else’s work
concepts.text: An automation script may own two settings while an operator owns the surrounding comments and other values. Repeatedly appending settings creates duplicates. Instead, retain unrelated lines, replace the settings you own and produce a predictable complete file. The worked report example owns style= and layout=; your later assignment owns different keys.

concepts.title: Keep literal lines, including their spaces
concepts.text: Use the supported IFS= read -r line idiom: empty IFS prevents surrounding spaces and tabs from being trimmed; -r keeps backslashes literal. while IFS= read -r line || test -n "$line" also handles a final nonempty record without LF. Redirect the loop with done < report.conf so its working variables remain in the caller; a pipeline loop has isolated variables. Here every retained record gets one ending LF.

concepts.title: Build a candidate before changing the file
concepts.text: case "$line" in style=*|layout=*) identifies the worked example’s two exact prefixes. Skip those old records and retain every other line in order, including blank records. Append exactly one desired style and layout pair. A name such as Style= or a line beginning with a space is unrelated data in this deliberately simple format.

concepts.title: Compare exact text without losing its final newlines
concepts.text: Command capture normally removes trailing LF characters. before=$(cat report.conf; printf '.') puts a non-newline marker after the file text, so capture keeps the real ending. Compare that value with "${candidate}." using the same marker. The marker is comparison data only; never write it into the configuration. Quoted values preserve literal text.

concepts.title: A second application should have nothing left to change
concepts.text: Idempotent means that applying the same desired settings again leaves equivalent file content. The example calls its helper twice inside one Run: the first reports Updated and the second Unchanged. This is actual shared file state within that evaluation. A new Run starts with its own sample files; it does not resume the previous Run’s files.

concepts.title: Validate, preview and report honestly
concepts.text: Check the interface before any write. After building a complete candidate, compare it with the original: unchanged is a useful result, not a failure. Preview shows a proposed change without publishing it; apply writes it. Preserve unrelated files and keep diagnostics on stderr. This teaches deterministic content repair, not real service configuration, atomic publication or recovery from a crash.

context: After exact text comparison, quoted arguments, Bash lists, complete line input and safe file publication. The lab supplies sample arguments and files; create your own working variables. Learn uses a separate example before the independent assignment.

Print Saved: N files followed by a newline on stdout, with N equal to the number of requested files. Success has status 0 and empty stderr; each error message also ends with a newline.

Preserve all source files and all unrelated files, and leave no extra files. This assignment makes content copies in the simulated flat file area; it is not an archive or a metadata-preserving filesystem snapshot.

goal: Correlate changing event evidence with a validated owner registry, while keeping incomplete analysis visible.
requirements: Read exactly two arguments: the owner-registry filename and event filename. Otherwise print Usage: triage OWNERS EVENTS and a newline to standard error, return status 2 and print no report.

Check that the owner file exists, then that the event file exists. Print Owner file is missing. or Event file is missing. and a newline to standard error for the first missing input; return 2 with no report.

Validate the entire owner registry before reporting events. Each row is device|owner: exactly one bar, a device matching [a-z][a-z0-9-]{0,31}, and a nonempty owner. On the first invalid row print Invalid owner row: N and a newline to standard error and return 2 with no report. On the first repeated device print Duplicate device: DEVICE instead and return 2 with no report. Count rows from 1. An empty registry is valid; owners containing only spaces are nonempty and must remain literal.

An event row has exactly three fields LEVEL|device|message. LEVEL is INFO, WARN or ERROR; the device follows the same rule as the registry, and message may be empty. Count every event row from 1, including INFO and malformed rows. For a malformed row print Skipped row N: malformed event and a newline to standard error, count one skipped row and continue.

Ignore valid INFO rows, including devices without owners. For a valid WARN or ERROR row with no owner print Unassigned row N: DEVICE and a newline to standard error, count one skipped row and continue. Otherwise print LEVEL|device|owner|message and a newline to standard output, in event order; count one reported row. Preserve literal spaces, backslashes, percent signs and other field text.

After processing events print Reported: N and Skipped: N on separate standard-output lines. Return 1 if any event rows were skipped, otherwise 0. Empty input produces both zero counts. Keep a final record without a newline. Never change or create any simulated file.

Inputs are finite UTF-8 text in the supplied flat virtual workspace: at most 8 rows per input, filenames at most 80 bytes, fields at most 128 bytes and no embedded newline or NUL. Bar characters are separators, not quoting or escaping. Support supplied filenames with spaces and literal wildcard characters; no host paths or general CSV parser are required.

goal: Read two observations, verify their source and calculate whole bytes per second over the actual interval.
context: Review quoted field selection, functions, integer arithmetic and file input. The lab supplies before.csv and after.csv; your script creates the variables it needs. No shell variables or host measurements are supplied implicitly.

concepts.title: A counter is a total so far
concepts.text: An interface counter counts bytes accumulated so far, not bytes per second. Subtract the earlier value from the later value to find how many bytes arrived or left during that interval. A large total can still describe a quiet interval.

concepts.title: Match the two observations
concepts.text: Each supplied one-line record has five comma-separated fields: boot label, interface name, time in milliseconds, received bytes and transmitted bytes. Match both the boot label and interface before subtracting. Different boots or interfaces do not describe one continuous counter.

concepts.title: Read the fields without running their text
concepts.text: Use quoted text with cut -d , -f NUMBER to select one field. The space after -d is required by this simulator subset. A function can reuse that selection. These lab records have exactly five fields and ordinary decimal whole numbers, with no leading zeros except 0 itself; they are not general quoted CSV.

concepts.title: Convert milliseconds to seconds
concepts.text: One second contains 1000 milliseconds. For elapsed milliseconds, bytes per second = byte change × 1000 ÷ elapsed. Multiply before dividing so an interval shorter than one second still works. Integer division rounds nonnegative results down to whole bytes per second.

concepts.title: Reject an interval that cannot be measured
concepts.text: Check source identity first, then require a later time, then reject either decreasing byte counter. Do those checks before division. A repeated timestamp is not zero traffic, and a reset or wrap is not a negative transfer rate. Equal counters over a positive interval are a valid measured zero.

requirements: Read before.csv and after.csv. Each contains one five-field record: boot,interface,time_ms,rx_bytes,tx_bytes; numeric fields are canonical decimal integers from 0 to 999999.
If boot labels or interface names differ, print Different source to stderr, followed by a newline, return 2 and print nothing to stdout.
Otherwise, if the later time is not greater, print Invalid interval to stderr with a newline, return 2 and print nothing to stdout.
Otherwise, if either byte counter decreases, print Counter reset to stderr with a newline, return 2 and print nothing to stdout.
For a valid pair, print one line INTERFACE rx=R B/s tx=T B/s, replacing INTERFACE with the supplied interface and R/T with whole per-second rates rounded down. Return 0 with no stderr.
Preserve every supplied file exactly and create no extra files. Each test starts with its own sample inputs and reset simulated files.

goal: Separate executing work from idle, wait and steal using changes in all supplied CPU categories.
context: Review the counter-rate lesson and integer arithmetic. before.csv and after.csv contain eight CPU counters from the same supplied source. Your script creates its own totals and temporary variables; these are not pre-filled environment values.

concepts.title: Read time accumulated in each category
concepts.text: Each counter counts time so far in ticks. These simplified one-line records use this order: user, nice, system, idle, iowait, irq, softirq, steal. They are lab CSV records, not the full text of /proc/stat. Subtract the before counter in every column before combining categories.

concepts.title: Decide what the CPU was executing
concepts.text: For this report, executing work is user + nice + system + irq + softirq. Nice time still means a process ran; hardware/software interrupt handling also uses CPU time. Keep idle, I/O-wait accounting and steal separate from executing work.

concepts.title: Use one interval denominator
concepts.text: Add all eight nonnegative counter changes to get the interval total. Divide each group by that same total and multiply by 100. This is an aggregate CPU share normalized to 100%, not a single-process percentage that can span several cores.

concepts.title: Report whole percentages honestly
concepts.text: Use (group change × 100) / total. Integer division drops the fractional part, so separately rounded fields can add to 99 rather than 100. In a printf format, %% prints a literal percent sign; %s inserts the quoted calculated value.

concepts.title: Distinguish missing measurement from idle
concepts.text: If any category decreases, reject the pair rather than silently changing that difference to zero. Real Linux I/O-wait accounting can decrease, so a decrease alone does not prove a reboot. If the total change is zero there is no CPU interval to report. A positive interval containing only idle ticks is valid 0% executing work.

requirements: Read before.csv and after.csv. Each contains one eight-field record in this order: user,nice,system,idle,iowait,irq,softirq,steal. All fields are canonical decimal integers from 0 to 999999; the source identity is already matched.
If any after counter is less than its before counter, print Counter decreased to stderr with a newline, return 2 and print no stdout.
Otherwise, if all counter changes total zero, print CPU counters did not advance to stderr with a newline, return 2 and print no stdout.

For a valid pair, compute work from user + nice + system + irq + softirq changes. Keep idle, wait and steal as separate groups. Normalize every group by the sum of all eight changes, rounding down to whole percent.
Print one line work=W% idle=I% wait=Q% steal=S%, replacing the uppercase letters with the four percentages. Return 0 with no stderr.
Preserve every supplied file exactly and create no extra files. Do not force rounded percentages to add to 100.

goal: Debug a streamed report that loses its final record, crosses invalid baselines and hides warnings.
context: Review both measurement lessons, full-line/EOF input, ERE validation, status handling and indexed lists. This capstone combines them. The supplied observations.csv and old report.txt are simulated files; keep.txt and the input must remain exact.

concepts.title: Treat the next row as a new observation
concepts.text: Each row contains boot,time_ms, then the eight CPU counters in their taught order, then rx_bytes,tx_bytes. There are twelve comma-separated fields for one fixed interface/CPU inventory. Compare adjacent valid rows, not every row with the first row or the boot totals.

concepts.title: Validate text before arithmetic
concepts.text: A boot label starts with a lowercase letter and continues with lowercase letters, digits or hyphens, at most 16 characters. Each numeric field is 0 or a 1–6 digit ordinary decimal integer without leading zeros. Reject a malformed row before arithmetic and clear the previous baseline: do not bridge across unknown data.

concepts.title: A bad pair can still supply the next baseline
concepts.text: For two well-formed rows, check boot identity, increasing time, nondecreasing counters, then positive CPU total, in that order. Skip an invalid pair and explain why. Keep its later row as the next baseline, so a following compatible pair can recover instead of silently disappearing.

concepts.title: Keep every final record
concepts.text: Use the full-line read and final-unterminated-record idiom from earlier lessons. The input loop must consume the entire finite file. No newline at the end does not make the last observation disposable. One valid row alone cannot produce a measurement window.

concepts.title: Accumulate a report without running its values
concepts.text: One Bash-specific approach is a dense indexed list: rebuild it with records=("${records[@]}" "$entry"), then print each quoted element using %s. Do not use += or computed-index operations: they are outside this simulator subset. A supported portable text accumulator is equally valid; the grade checks behavior, not which approach you choose.

concepts.title: Tell warnings from code failures
concepts.text: Write a labeled report containing valid intervals and warning counts. Exit 0 means no warnings, 1 means some records/pairs were rejected but useful windows remain, and 2 means none could be measured. A test can correctly expect 1 or 2; matching that required rejection passes. Syntax/unsupported-feature errors remain code failures, not data warnings.

requirements: Repair the supplied script for observations.csv. Each row has twelve fields: boot,time_ms,user,nice,system,idle,iowait,irq,softirq,steal,rx_bytes,tx_bytes. The interface and CPU inventory are fixed.

A boot label matches [a-z][a-z0-9-]{0,15}; each numeric field is 0 or [1-9][0-9]{0,5}. For any malformed row print Skipped malformed record to stderr with a newline, count one warning and clear the previous baseline.

The first well-formed row after startup or malformed data becomes a baseline. For each following well-formed row, check boot identity, increasing time, nondecreasing CPU/network counters and nonzero CPU total, in that order.

Reject a bad pair with one stderr line: REASON at TIME; new baseline. REASON is Different boot, Time did not advance, Counter decreased or CPU counters did not advance, matching the first failed check. Count one warning and use the later row as the next baseline.

For every valid pair retain one report line BOOT@TIME cpu=P% rx=R B/s tx=T B/s. Use executing-work CPU share and whole per-second byte rates as taught, rounding down. Keep valid lines in observation order and process an unterminated final record.

Replace report.txt with Measurement report on its first line, then all valid report lines, then Valid windows: N and Warnings: M on separate lines. End each line with a newline, including an empty-data report; do not retain stale report text.
Print one stdout line Report: N valid windows, M rejected records or intervals. Return 0 when at least one valid window and no warnings remain, or 1 when useful windows remain with warnings.
If no valid window remains, also print Not enough compatible observations to stderr with a newline and return 2, after writing the zero-window report and stdout summary.
Preserve observations.csv and keep.txt byte for byte and create no extra files. Equivalent supported solutions pass; an indexed array is optional.
